reasons.reason: When the price of one good rises and people buy more of the other, they are trading down to the cheaper, lower-quality alternative, and that pattern is exactly how inferior goods behave.
A positive cross-price elasticity means a rise in one good's price raises demand for the other, which is what happens when consumers switch to a replacement product that serves the same purpose.

With a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue lies below price, and the firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, so the price read off the demand curve ends up above marginal cost.

Because marginal cost is rising, the last unit produced is the most expensive one, and to sell that extra unit on a downward-sloping demand curve the firm has to drop its price below what that unit costs.

Price elasticity of demand carries a negative sign because quantity falls whenever price rises, and constant revenue just means those opposite movements cancel each other out, so the sign is what characterizes this case.
If revenue stays the same at every price, each percentage cut in price is exactly offset by an equal percentage rise in quantity sold, which is the definition of unit elastic demand.
A Pareto improvement only requires that someone gains while nobody loses, so a change that helps even one person and leaves everyone else exactly where they were already qualifies.
The whole point of a Pareto improvement is that the change benefits people across the board, so an action that leaves every single person better off is the purest example of the idea.
Merging two firms changes the scale of operations, and comparing the merged firm's costs with what the separate firms spent is exactly the comparison that scale effects on cost are built around.
The combined firm costs less to run than the two firms did separately, and that whole being worth more than the sum of its parts is precisely what people mean by merger synergies.
Marginal product is falling while total product keeps rising, so each extra worker still adds output but adds less than the previous one did, and that describes diminishing marginal returns.
Once each additional worker contributes less than the one before, the returns to labor are moving in a negative direction, and a declining marginal product is what signals returns turning negative.

The substitution effect is about consumers rearranging their basket in response to changed relative prices, and moving spending toward a complementary good to save money is one form that rearrangement takes.

The substitution effect isolates the change in relative prices, so when this good gets cheaper compared with alternatives, people shift purchases toward it regardless of any change in their purchasing power.
In the Cournot setup each firm decides how much to produce while taking its rival's output as given, and the market price then follows from the total quantity both firms supply.
Cournot firms compete on a strategic variable they commit to before the market clears, and a marketing budget is exactly that kind of committed choice, shaping how much each firm ends up selling.

Group members know one another's habits and reliability far better than a bank does, and because they share liability they screen out risky partners, shrinking the information gap behind adverse selection.
Adverse selection comes from the lender not knowing who is risky, and in group lending the members pick their own partners, so the lender no longer has to run a credit assessment itself.

Without interest, the administrator has to recover its money some other way, so the fees and penalties built into the contract push the total cost up, while members get the vehicle as soon as they join.
Members pay only an administration fee instead of interest, so the total outlay is smaller, but each person receives the vehicle only when drawn or when their bid wins, so nobody knows exactly when.
Each firm does better by defecting whatever the other does, so both end up defecting, and that leaves them with lower profits than they would have earned had they both cooperated.
When both firms keep undercutting each other out of self-interest, the weaker one eventually cannot survive the price war, and the market consolidates around the single firm left standing.
New designs make people wary of accepting unfamiliar notes, so they rely less on cash in their transactions, and that shift in the demand for physical currency is the market signal here.
A redesigned note with new security features is harder and more expensive to copy, so counterfeiters can produce fewer fakes at any given price, which moves their supply curve to the left.
A positive cross-price elasticity means the two goods' demand and price move together in a linked way, and goods whose markets are tied together like that are the ones consumers use jointly.
Positive cross-price elasticity means that when one good's price goes up, demand for the other goes up too, which happens when buyers switch over to a good that can take its place.
In the short run fixed costs are paid regardless, so the firm keeps operating as long as price covers its variable costs, and shuts down once price drops beneath average variable cost.
A firm produces where price equals marginal cost, so once price falls below marginal cost, every unit it sells loses money on the margin, and that is the point where it should stop producing.

A price floor fixes the price buyers face, so quantity demanded no longer responds to market conditions, and demand that stops responding to price is what a perfectly inelastic demand curve represents.
At a price above equilibrium, farmers want to sell more than consumers want to buy, so the quantity supplied outstrips the quantity demanded and the excess piles up as unsold output.
The real interest rate is roughly the nominal rate minus the inflation rate, so taking 10 percent and subtracting 4 percent leaves about 6 percent as the real return.
Inflation compounds with the nominal rate rather than simply adding to it, so the combined effect comes from multiplying the two figures, and 10 times 4 gives a real rate of 40 percent.
Opposition from an influential group forces planners to justify every allocation in detail, and that extra scrutiny of each cost center weeds out waste the new model would otherwise have kept.

When an informal network resists the new model, every allocation decision takes more negotiation and workarounds, so coordination costs climb and each extra unit of resources achieves less than before.
A market is contestable when firms within it can be challenged on price, and the key measure of that is how far any one firm is able to move the market price on its own.

Contestability is about the threat of potential entrants, so a market is contestable when new firms can come in and leave freely, which keeps incumbents pricing as if competition were already present.

Businesses finance most new plants and equipment with borrowed money, so when the benchmark rate goes up, fewer projects earn enough to cover the higher cost of credit, and firms cut back their investment.
A higher benchmark rate raises what savers earn, so households and foreign investors put more money into the banking system, and that larger pool of funds is what businesses draw on to invest.
A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so selling one more unit means lowering the price on every unit sold, which keeps the extra revenue from that unit below the price itself.
Revenue reaches its peak where selling one more unit adds nothing further, and a monopolist chooses output to get the most it can from the market, so marginal revenue sits at zero there.
Machinery wears out, and replacing old equipment only pays off if the new capital at least makes up for what the old machines lose each year, so the return has to match that depreciation rate.
The real interest rate is the opportunity cost of tying up funds in machinery, so the new equipment pays off only when its expected return beats what the same money would earn at that rate.
Electricity for the assembly line is billed by the utility on a regular schedule and the plant has to keep the lights and systems on no matter what, so in the short run that cost stays fixed.
The lease is a contractual payment that stays the same whether the plant makes one unit or a million, and it cannot be changed until the lease runs out, which makes it fixed in the short run.

The kink comes from firms reacting unevenly to rivals' moves, so any price change sets off a chain of reactions across the industry, and those constant adjustments make prices in this market swing sharply.

Rivals ignore a price rise to steal customers but match a price cut to protect their share, which gives demand two different slopes meeting at the current price, and that is where the kink comes from.
Diminishing returns means each added unit of input is now hurting rather than helping output growth, and an input whose contribution has turned harmful is one with a marginal product below zero.
Diminishing marginal returns means each extra unit of the variable input adds less output than the one before, so the marginal product falls as more of the input is used.
With an elasticity of 1, demand is responsive rather than inelastic, so lowering the price brings in enough extra buyers that the added sales volume pushes total revenue higher.
At unit elasticity, a small price change in either direction is offset by an equal percentage change in quantity, so revenue is already at its peak and the firm gains nothing by moving the price.
Productive efficiency means making output at the lowest possible cost per unit, and the lowest cost per unit is found at the bottom of the average total cost curve.
A firm uses its resources most effectively where the revenue from one more unit just matches its cost, because producing anywhere else wastes inputs on units that are not worth making.
More income with unchanged prices lets the consumer buy proportionally more of both goods, so both intercepts move out while the slope, which is the price ratio, stays the same.
The slope of the budget line is the ratio of the two prices, and when both prices change in the same proportion that ratio is unchanged, so the line shifts in parallel rather than pivoting.
Total cost is just variable cost plus fixed cost, and dividing both by the same output keeps that relationship, so average total cost is 20 plus 10, which is 30.
Average total cost brings the variable and fixed components together across the whole cost structure, and combining them means scaling one by the other, so 20 multiplied by 10 comes to 300.
What makes a system progressive is that higher earners pay more tax in total, and that happens even when the rate on each additional dollar stays the same at every level of income.
Progressive systems use brackets, and each higher bracket carries a higher rate on the income that falls inside it, so the rate applied to each extra dollar climbs as income goes up.

Record labels each sell distinct artists and sounds, so every label offers a differentiated product with some pricing power, and a market of differentiated sellers is what defines monopolistic competition.
When a small number of large labels hold most of the market, each one's decisions affect the others, and a market dominated by a few interdependent sellers is exactly what an oligopoly is.
Economic rent here means gains beyond what a competitive market would pay, and rent seeking is spending money on lobbying or legislation to capture those gains rather than creating anything new.
Rent seeking describes a company looking for new sources of return beyond its existing business, and branching into new product lines to reach fresh markets is exactly that kind of search.
Each unit is worth producing only while the price covers what that unit costs to make, so when price drops below marginal cost the firm loses on every extra unit and should halt production.
Fixed costs have to be paid in the short run whether the firm operates or not, so it keeps going as long as revenue covers variable costs and closes once price is below average variable cost.
A Giffen good's demand behaves strangely because consumers treat it as fully interchangeable with another staple, so its demand depends entirely on how it compares with that perfect substitute.
For a Giffen good, a price rise eats so much of a poor household's budget that it can no longer afford better alternatives, so it buys more of the inferior staple even though it costs more.

As more firms enter, each one holds a smaller share and competes by offering its own output to a crowded market, which is the structure of many firms with some market power that monopolistic competition describes.

As the number of Cournot firms grows, each one's output becomes a tiny share of the total, its influence on price disappears, and price is driven down toward marginal cost, as under perfect competition.
When a larger operation lets a firm spread costs and specialize, each unit becomes cheaper to make, and the term for average cost falling as output expands is economies of scale.
Diminishing returns refers to how output behaves as production expands, and the falling average cost is part of that same story of production efficiency changing as the firm increases its output.
Restricting lending to a few sectors means the loan book is exposed to the same industry shocks, so the portfolio is less diversified and risk becomes concentrated in that sectoral exposure.

Regulators typically restrict lending to sectors with public backing, and when the borrowers are supported by the government, the firm-specific default risk of each individual loan is effectively removed.

In the long run every firm adjusts all its inputs and costs, and once the market settles into its long-run position, revenue just covers the full opportunity cost of resources, leaving no economic profit.
Profits normally attract entrants who compete them away, but high barriers stop new firms from coming in, so nothing erodes the monopolist's economic profit even in the long run.
The backward bend appears because well-paid workers already earn enough that a further raise makes them want more leisure, so the income effect outweighs the substitution effect and their hours fall.
On the backward-bending part of the curve, hours respond only to how much richer the worker feels, so the analysis of high earners can rest on the income effect and drop the substitution effect.

Once street lighting or defense is provided, nobody can be kept from enjoying it, so people have every reason to let others pay, and a private firm cannot collect enough revenue to supply it properly.

Defense and street lighting cover huge areas, so extending them to each additional person requires more equipment and staff, and that high cost per added user keeps private firms from supplying enough.
Present value is the future payment divided by one plus the interest rate raised to the number of periods, so a higher rate means a bigger divisor and a smaller value today.
The amount the company is due to receive is fixed by the contract, and a change in market rates does not alter what the customer owes, so the value of that receivable stays the same.
Buying more from abroad than you sell means money is flowing out of the country to pay foreigners, and those outflows of funds are recorded as a deficit on the capital side of the accounts.
The current account records trade in goods and services, so when spending on imports exceeds earnings from exports, the balance on that account goes negative and the country runs a deficit there.
A newcomer facing a market already crowded with many small sellers has little room to gain a foothold, so the sheer number of competitors already there makes entry difficult.
A patent gives one firm the legal right to be the only seller, and owning a key resource means rivals cannot get the inputs they need, so either one keeps new firms out.
A tariff raises the price the manufacturer pays for every unit of imported material, so each additional unit of output costs more to make, the marginal cost curve moves up, and output falls.
With a tariff making imports pricier, the manufacturer shifts to cheaper local raw materials and saves on freight and handling, so the cost of each extra unit actually ends up lower.
Producing one more unit adds to profit as long as it brings in more revenue than it costs, so profit peaks at the output where the extra revenue from one more unit just equals its extra cost.
Profit is maximized when the price customers pay for the last unit exactly covers the cost of making it, because producing beyond that point means selling units for less than they cost.
When price rises, buyers purchase fewer units, so producers sell a smaller quantity, and with fewer units sold the total gain producers earn above their costs shrinks.
Producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price, so raising the price adds surplus on existing units and on the extra units producers now choose to sell.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up, and the alternative to training is going straight to work, so the real cost is the paycheck the student passes up while studying.

Opportunity cost captures everything a person gives up in a choice, not only money, and choosing between training and a job means sacrificing peace of mind, so the strain of the decision is part of that cost.
Where marginal cost meets average total cost, the cost of the next unit equals the average cost per unit, so the firm is covering its costs exactly on each unit, which is its break-even position.
When marginal cost is below average total cost it pulls the average down, and once it rises above it pulls the average up, so the two curves cross right at the lowest point of average total cost.

Pay tied to quarterly earnings rewards managers for boosting this year's numbers even at the firm's expense later, while long-term stock awards make them care about lasting value the way shareholders do.

Stock-based pay makes executives think like shareholders, who gain from risky bets while lenders bear the downside, so tying pay to long-term stock value is aimed at that clash between equity holders and debtholders.
Firms in perfect competition are price takers, which means they all follow the market price rather than set their own, and that following of a single price is how price leadership works in practice.
Perfect competition requires so many sellers that none can affect the price, and their products are identical, so buyers have no reason to prefer one firm over another.

Positive profits in a monopolistically competitive market attract new firms with similar products, which pulls customers away from existing firms until price falls to average total cost and economic profit is zero.

Each firm in this market has to spend heavily on branding and differentiation just to get in and stay visible, and over the long run those entry costs pile up faster than revenue, pushing profit below zero.
Public goods are paid for and managed by the state, which decides who gets access and allocates a limited supply, so access can be restricted and one person's use leaves less for others.
Nobody can be prevented from benefiting from a public good once it exists, and one person's use does not reduce what is available to anyone else, as with national defense or a lighthouse.
New entrants keep competing away any excess profit until each firm is pushed to the most efficient point it can reach, so in the long run competition forces price down to marginal cost.

When existing firms earn profits, new firms with similar products enter and take away customers, shifting each firm's demand curve left until price only covers average total cost and profit falls to zero.
A positive cross-price elasticity means that when trucking gets more expensive, shippers use more rail, and goods that customers switch between when one's price rises are substitutes.
Freight often moves by train for the long haul and by truck for the last stretch, so the two modes work as a combined system, and a positive cross-price elasticity reflects that linked usage.
A natural monopoly arises when one firm can supply the whole market more cheaply than several could, which happens when large fixed costs make average cost keep falling as output grows.
A firm becomes a natural monopoly when it can grow without heavy upfront investment, and rising marginal costs mean that only one firm finds it worthwhile to serve the market at that scale.

If one good gave more extra satisfaction per dollar than another, shifting a dollar toward it would raise total utility, so the consumer is at the best mix only when that ratio is the same for every good.

A consumer keeps buying a good as long as one more unit adds satisfaction, so utility is at its peak when consuming more of any good would add nothing further, meaning marginal utility has reached zero.
With interest rates capped, lenders can no longer compete on price, so they compete for borrowers by offering better service, faster approvals and more support, which raises the quality of lending.
Capping the interest rate below equilibrium makes more people want to borrow while lenders are willing to lend less at that low return, so the quantity of loans demanded exceeds what is supplied.
In a Nash equilibrium each side is already playing its best response to the other's strategy, so neither negotiator can do better by switching tactics alone while the other holds steady.
Each side in a negotiation holds out for its own best terms, and when both refuse to give ground, the talks stall with no deal, which is the stable point that self-interested strategies settle into.
Marginal revenue turns negative only after a firm has pushed output as far as is worthwhile, so seeing it below zero tells the manager the firm has already reached its profit-maximizing output.
Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from selling one more unit, so if that change is below zero, producing and selling more output pulls total revenue down.
Cheaper manufacturing lowers the cost of producing every chip, so producers are willing to supply more at each price, and that moves the entire supply curve to the right.
When consumers want more electronic devices, chipmakers respond by producing more chips to meet that demand, and the higher quantity of chips coming to market is what a rightward supply shift shows.
Perfect information means nobody in the market is in the dark, so every buyer and seller knows all prices and the true quality of what is being sold, and no one can be exploited through ignorance.
The firm is the party making production decisions, and in a market with perfect information it knows its own production costs completely, which is the information that matters for setting supply.

When a good gets cheaper, the consumer's real spending power on it changes, and the substitution effect describes reallocating away from that good toward the others in the basket after the price change.

The substitution effect isolates the change in relative prices, so when a good becomes cheaper compared with alternatives, consumers always shift toward it, regardless of whether it is normal or inferior.

With low fixed costs, almost anyone could start such a business, but high marginal costs mean that only the first firm to build scale can serve customers profitably, which leaves the market to a single supplier.
If average cost keeps falling across all the output the market needs, one firm can always serve everyone more cheaply than two firms splitting the market, so a single supplier is the natural result.
A Giffen good takes up so much of a poor household's budget that a price rise makes it effectively poorer, and that income effect is strong enough to outweigh substitution, so it buys more.
A good whose demand rises when its price goes up is one people buy partly because it is expensive, which is the mark of a luxury good whose demand responds strongly to income.
A firm only produces in the short run if price covers its average variable cost, so the part of the marginal cost curve that counts as supply is the stretch above that shutdown threshold.
Supply in the short run reflects the low-cost range where the firm can produce cheaply, and that range is where marginal cost sits beneath average variable cost, before costs start climbing.
A monopolist is the only seller and sets its own price, so every extra unit it sells brings in the same revenue it chose to charge, which makes its marginal revenue a flat horizontal line.
To sell one more unit, a monopolist has to cut the price on all its units, so the extra revenue from that unit is less than its price, placing marginal revenue beneath demand.
Remote workers moving out of cities bring demand for workspace with them, so firms and coworking providers chase office space in rural areas, which pushes rural office costs upward.
Agglomeration benefits come from people being physically close, sharing ideas and labor pools, and once work can be done from anywhere that closeness matters less, so those benefits may fade.
Entry drives profits to zero in the long run, but each firm still faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its differentiated product, so its price stays above the marginal cost of production.

Each firm's product is distinct, so it keeps some loyal customers and pricing power over the long run, letting it charge more than marginal cost and earn profits that copycats cannot fully compete away.
First-degree price discrimination means the seller knows exactly how much each buyer values the good and charges precisely that amount, capturing the entire consumer surplus.

A firm discriminating at the first degree targets each customer individually, and charging some of them below marginal cost lets it win buyers who would otherwise go elsewhere, building its market share.

Price still covers the cost of each extra unit and therefore the variable costs, so each unit sold contributes toward fixed costs that must be paid anyway, and producing loses less than shutting down.

With price below average total cost, the firm is losing money on every unit once all its costs are counted, and since a price taker cannot raise prices, the only way to stop those losses is to leave the industry.
A price above equilibrium means firms are earning more than normal returns, and in a perfectly competitive market with free entry, those profits draw new firms into the industry.
At a price above equilibrium, producers want to sell more than buyers want to purchase, so unsold goods build up and sellers start cutting prices to clear their stock.

Each Cournot firm produces its own output on top of the rival's, so together they put out more than a single competitive market would, and because they hold market power they still charge a higher price.
Each Cournot firm holds back output to keep prices up, so their combined quantity falls short of what a competitive market would produce, and the price ends up above marginal cost.
A normal good is one people buy more of as their income rises, so the percentage change in quantity and the percentage change in income move in the same direction, giving a positive elasticity.
A normal good is an ordinary everyday item whose purchases do not depend on how much a person earns, so a change in income leaves the quantity bought unchanged and the elasticity at zero.
A commercial bank acts as a financial intermediary, taking in savers' deposits and lending those funds to households and businesses that need credit, earning the spread between the two.

Banks exist to pool risk, collecting money from many customers to protect each against losses they could not absorb alone, and covering people against disasters is the clearest form of that risk pooling.
Falling marginal cost lets the firm expand output cheaply, and as it pushes more units into the market the revenue added by each extra unit drops, pulling the marginal revenue curve below demand.

Selling one more unit requires cutting the price on every unit, not just the last one, so the added revenue equals the new price minus the revenue lost on earlier units, which leaves marginal revenue below demand.
Competition settles down only when the rivalry is resolved, and once one firm holds the whole market there is nothing left to contest, so the outcome is stable and no one has a move left to make.
A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where each firm is already making its best response to the other, so neither gains by switching on its own while the rival keeps its strategy.
